analytic.title: Geographical variation in body size of a pelagic seabird, the streaked shearwater Calonectris leucomelas

div.head: Aim
div.p: In general, within temperate latitudes, races of endotherms tend to show larger body size at higher latitudes, while smaller-bodied ones tend to be found at lower latitudes, a pattern known as Bergmann's rule (or James's rule for intra-specific patterns). The adaptive basis of this geographic variation in body size is explained mostly by the heat conservation hypothesis. Application of Bergmann's rule has been confirmed mostly among terrestrial taxa and studies of marine taxa are rare. Our aim was to examine whether the intra-specific variation in body size of a pelagic seabird species (streaked shearwater Calonectris leucomelas) follows Bergmann's/James's rule.
Location Eight different breeding colonies of the streaked shearwater, ranging from 24-39°N in latitude (approximately the full latitudinal range of the species) and 142-123°E in longitude.

div.head: Methods
div.p: We measured morphological traits of 454 adult streaked shearwaters in total.

Principal components analysis was used to create a composite body size index for each sex from each colony using the measured traits, and the value of first principal component was compared. The relationships between body size index and latitude, longitude and the averaged mean air temperature were examined using generalized linear models.

div.head: Results
div.p: Body size was positively correlated with latitude and longitude, and negatively correlated with the mean air temperature. Latitude and longitude were highly correlated with air temperature. Nonetheless, between colonies, populations that are considered to 4 4 forage over large areas appeared to exhibit smaller body size than those of lower latitude populations.

div.head: Main conclusion
div.p: The overall trend of the geographical variations in body size of streaked shearwaters followed Bergmann's/James's rule, suggesting that this rule may be applicable to seabirds. However, in addition to thermoregulatory adaptation, intra-specific differences in foraging characteristic in relation to local marine environment might also affect the body size in highly mobile seabirds.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: There has been a widely supported hypothesis that mean body size of endothermic races tends to be larger within temperate latitudes where conditions within the range are cooler, which manifests in a cline of increasing body size with latitude: this is known as Bergman's rule at the inter-specific level (Bergmann, 1847cited in Blackburn, et al., 1999) or James's rule for intra-specific pattern (Rensch, 1938;James, 1970). Latitudinal gradients in body size are primarily explained by the heat conservation hypothesis (James, 1970;Blackburn, et al., 1999;Blackburn & Hawkins, 2004). The surface area to volume ratio is lower in large-bodied animals, so they are better able to conserve heat in cooler climates at higher latitudes. Climate varies both latitudinally and longitudinally. Hence, body size can also vary with longitude (Thurber & Peterson, 1991;Wojczulanis-Jakubas et al., 2011).

Most evidence for a geographic pattern in body size derives from studies of terrestrial taxa, including mammals (Ashton et al., 2000;Meiri & Dayan, 2003;Blackburn & Hawkins, 2004;Rodríguez et al., 2008) and birds (Blackburn & Gaston, 1996;Ashton, 2002;Meiri & Dayan, 2003;Olson, et al., 2009), although a few studies have also reported a similar clinal trend in marine taxa (Brunner, 2002;Wojczulanis-Jakubas et al., 2011).

Procellariiformes (albatrosses, petrels, and shearwaters) are seabirds that travel large distances at sea, but return to specific locations to reproduce, usually on isolated islands (Warham, 1990). Populations that are spatially disjunct may be expected to generate inter-colony differences in morphological characteristic (Moen, 1991;Barrett et al., 1997;Waugh et al., 1999;Bull, 2006;Einoder et al., 2008). However, within-species comparisons of body size in seabirds have often been limited to two or three populations, usually due to the inaccessibility to their breeding locations (e.g. on isolated islands and/or at cliffs), and therefore do not cover their full breeding range. Hence, a comprehensive analysis of body size variation across a species' full geographical range has rarely been performed for pelagic seabird species (Wojczulanis-Jakubas et al., 2011).
The streaked shearwater (Calonectris leucomelas) breeds on isolated islands in east and southeast Asia from April to early November (Yoshida, 1981;Oka, 2004).

Breeding colonies of this species are distributed widely from 24 °N to 42 °N in latitude and from 121 °E to 142 °E in longitude, hence characteristics of the local environment differ substantially between colonies (Yamamoto et al., 2011(Yamamoto et al., , 2012)). For example, Oka (2004) reported that sea surface temperature in spring (average monthly mean in March during 1980s-1990s) vary from 1 °C to 25 °C among colonies within the breeding range. Previous 6 studies have reported body size measurements of this shearwater species in different breeding colonies (on Kanmurijima and Mikurajima, Arima & Sugawa, 2004;Ochi et al., 2010;Arima et al., 2014), indicating that there may be inter-colony differences in their morphological size (Arima et al., 2014), but a comprehensive analysis of their body size across the full breeding range has not been performed.

Here, we measured the external morphology of streaked shearwaters at eight different breeding colonies around Japan ranging from 24-39°N in latitude and 123-142°E in longitude. Our aims were to explore the inter-colony variation in body size of this pelagic seabird species, and, then, to examine if the variation follows Bergmann's/James's rule. As males are larger than females in streaked shearwaters (Arima & Sugawa, 2004;Arima et al., 2014) sexual dimorphism may influence the pattern of inter-colony variation in body size. Therefore, we analysed that issue first, and then treated males and females separately in the further analyses.

div.head: MATERIALS AND METHODS
div.p: We measured adult streaked shearwaters during the incubation or chick-rearing period (August-October) in 2006-2013 at eight islands in Japan that vary substantially in latitude: Funakoshi-Ohshima (hereafter FO), which is one of the northernmost colonies for the species, Sanganjima (SA), Awashima (AW), Kanmurijima (KA), Mikurajima (MI), Uwashima (UW), Danjo-gunto (DA), and Nakanokamishima (NA), which is one of the southernmost colonies (see Fig. 1 for the location of each colony). The breeding populations were estimated to be <1,000 birds at FO (Oka, 2004), 109,000 birds at SA (Matsumoto et al., 2007), 61,000 birds at AW (M. Yamamoto, unpublished data), 240,000 birds at KA (Yoshida, 1981;Oka, 2004), 770,000 birds at MI (Japanese Ministry of the Environment, 2013), <100 birds at UW (S. Watanabe, personal communication), several thousand birds at DA (Oka, 2004), and ca. 5,500 birds at NA (Yamamoto et al., 2015).

Body mass was measured using a 1 kg spring balance to the nearest 1 g. Bill length, bill depth, total head length, and tarsus length were measured using a Vernier caliper to the nearest 0.1 mm (see Fig. 2 in Arima & Sugawa, 2004 for the measurement parts), and wing length was measured with a ruler to the nearest 1 mm, for a total of 454 birds from eight breeding colonies (see Table 1 and Appendix S1 in Supporting Information). To minimize errors (Bailey & Byrnes, 1990), each measurement was repeated 2 or 3 times, and the average value was used. Most measurements were undertaken by T. Yamamoto (400 out of 454 birds), but some were done by co-authors (34 birds at UW by S. Watanabe and 20 birds at DA by K. Yoda and S. Matsumoto) following the same method previously confirmed between the authors. We determined the sex of all the birds based on their vocalizations during handling; the calls of males are high pitched, whereas those of females are low pitched (Arima & Sugawa, 2004;Arima et al., 2014). Some birds did not call voluntarily during the handling, and, then, we pushed their abdomen gently once or twice in accordance with breathing to produce a call.

We compared the sexual size difference (SSD) in streaked shearwaters using the formula: SSD = M ave /F ave (Smith, 1999), where M ave and F ave is the mean value of each morphological trait (bill length, bill depth, total head length, wing length, and tarsus length) in males and females of a given colony, respectively.

Principal components analysis (PCA) was used to create a composite body size index for each sex from each colony. Body size index was derived by incorporating measures of five parameters (bill length, bill depth, total head length, tarsus length, and wing length). We excluded body mass from the PCA of individuals, because body mass can vary depending on the breeding phase (i.e. shearwaters fast for up to several days during the incubation duty: Yamamoto et al., 2012) and the timing of capture (i.e. before/after feeding a chick: Ochi et al., 2010). Collectively, the first principal component (PC1) explained 75.2% of the variance in body size (see Appendix S2 for the relationship between PC1 and each of the input variables).

Differences in body size between sexes and among colonies were compared using Mann-Whitney U tests and Kruskal-Wallis rank sum tests with a Bonferroni post hoc test for multiple comparisons, respectively (Zar, 1999). To test Bergmann's rule, the relationships between body size and latitude/longitude/air temperatures were examined using generalized linear models (GLM) with a Gaussian error distribution. We also examined the relationships without NA, because the outlier may affect the result of linear regression and/or to confirm that the relationship still existed within a narrower range of latitude (31!39°N).

The averaged mean air temperature in July-September (during incubation and chick-rearing periods for streaked shearwaters) in 1981-2010 was obtained from the Japan Meteorological Agency (available at www.jma.go.jp), and data measured at a meteorological station closest to each colony were used; <30 km from the colony except DA (c. 70 km).

The PCA were performed in Minitab (version 14.20,Minitab Inc.). Other statistical analysis were conducted in R software (version 2.5.1, R Development Core Team, 2008). Values are presented as the mean ± SD and statistical significance was set at <0.05.

div.head: RESULTS
div.p: Male streaked shearwaters had a significantly larger body size index than females at all the study colonies (Mann-Whitney U tests, all Z > 3.21, P " 0.001, Table 1, Fig. 2). Bill depth was the trait showing the largest difference between sexes, being 1.08-1.16 times larger in males than females (Table 2). Furthermore, SSD in bill depth exhibited a relatively large variation among the colonies, as standard deviation for bill depth was 0.03, compared to other traits (SD = 0.01) (Table 2).

Overall, geographical variation in body size was positively correlated with latitude [male: Y = 1.16X + 197.5 (R 2 = 0.67, P < 0.001), female: Y = 1.20X + 186.6 (R 2 = 0.69, P < 0.001)] and longitude [male: Y = 0.87X + 119.0 (R 2 = 0.58, P < 0.001), female: Y = 0.88X + 108.4 (R 2 = 0.58, P < 0.001)], and negatively correlated with air temperature [male: Y = -2.25X + 291.6 (R 2 = 0.58, P < 0.001), females: Y = -2.26X + 282.9 (R 2 = 0.55, P < 0.001)] (Fig. 2). Both latitude and longitude were highly correlated with air temperature [Pearson's correlation coefficient, latitudevs. temperature: -0.91 (P < 0.001), longitude vs. temperature: -0.89 (P < 0.001)]. The coefficient of determination (R 2 ) decreased, especially for the longitude, when excluding NA, which possessed birds of smaller body size than the other study colonies [latitude: Y = 0.95X + 205.3 (R 2 = 0.22, P < 0.001) in male and Y = 0.70X + 205.5 (R 2 = 0.16, P < 0.001) in female, longitude: Y = 0.37X + 188.4 (R 2 = 0.06, P < 0.001) in male and Y = 0.27X + 193.3 (R 2 = 0.05, P < 0.001) in female, and air temperature: Y = -1.20X + 268.1 (R 2 = 0.20, P < 0.001) in male andY = -0.89X + 251.8 (R 2 = 0.14, P < 0.001) in female] (Fig. 2).
Body size index values differed among the colonies (Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test, 10 X 2 = 133.30, df = 7, P < 0.001 for males and X 2 = 135.75, df = 7, P < 0.001 for females).

FO males were significantly larger than MI males; SA birds larger than birds at KA, MI, and DA (SA females were also larger than UW females); AW birds larger than MI birds (AW females were also larger than KA females); and birds from all other colonies were significantly larger than NA birds (see Table 3).

div.head: DISCUSSION
div.p: Streaked shearwaters exhibit sexual size dimorphism in their morphology (Arima & Sugawa, 2004;Shirai et al., 2013;Arima et al., 2014), and we confirmed that males were larger than females in the overall body size and each morphological trait throughout all the study colonies. Bill depth was the most different trait between males and females, while the degree of SSD for bill depth appeared to vary among the colonies. Calonectris species commonly defend their nests against conspecifics by fighting (Warham, 1996), and a more robust bill could be advantageous to males for physical combat (Navarro et al., 2009a;Shirai et al., 2013). In streaked shearwaters, the competence of males for competition during the breeding period should be relevant; during pre-laying period males are probably responsible for nest defence against other prospecting birds, while females engage in offshore foraging to accumulate resources for egg production (Yamamoto et al., 2011).

Among the study colonies, individuals breeding in large populations (>60,000 birds: SA, AW, KA and MI) appeared to show relatively larger SSD compared to birds in small populations (less than several thousand birds: UW, DA, and NA, except FO) (Table 2).
Social interactions may affect bill morphology in streaked shearwaters through sexual selection (Navarro et al., 2009a).

We found that the body size of streaked shearwaters showed an overall increase from the south to north (and also from the west to east). Such a relationship between body size and latitude is in line with Bergmann's/James's rule, which describes a general pattern of larger-bodied individuals living at higher (cooler) latitudes and smaller-bodied individuals living at lower (warmer) latitudes (Bergmann, 1847;James, 1970;Blackburn et al., 1999). The adaptive basis of geographic variation in animals' body size has been explained mostly by the heat conservation hypothesis (Blackburn et al., 1999). Increased body size at higher latitudes is thought to reduce heat loss owing to a lower surface area to volume ratio that enables individuals to conserve heat in cooler climates. In this study, latitude and longitude were highly correlated with air temperature, and air temperature itself also showed a negative relationship with the body size. Hence, overall latitudinal and longitudinal trends in the body size of streaked shearwaters likely reflect adaptations to thermal conditions of each colony location (i.e. air temperature). Nonetheless, the coefficient of determination (R 2 ) became smaller when excluding NA from the analysis. This might suggest that there could be additional factors driving the variation in their body size, such as characteristics relating to foraging behaviour (cf. the resource availability hypothesis: Blackburn et al., 1999).

Among some colonies, the body size-latitude relationship appeared to be reversed; MI birds were smaller than UW and DA birds that breed at colonies of lower latitude, and UW birds were larger than higher latitude colony of KA (Fig. 2a), although these differences were not significant (Table 3). During the breeding period, MI shearwaters travel comparatively greater distances than shearwaters from other colonies (e.g. the mean maximum distance from the colony during the incubation period was 272 km for SA, 228 km for AW, and 645 km for MI : Yamamoto et al., 2012). In contrast, UW birds forage in a very small area (c. <150 km from the colony), mostly within the Seto Inland Sea (Ito et al., 2013). Smaller body size is thought to be adaptive for travelling great distances (for example as found in snow petrels Pagodroma nivea: Barbraud et al., 1999), while possible higher flight costs due to increased body size (i.e. lower surface area to volume ratio) could be offset by reduced travel time (Weimerskirch, 2007;Cairns et al., 2008). In this respect, differences in foraging behaviour may also determine, in part, the inter-colony variations in the body size, though foraging behaviour has not been examined in all of our study colonies.

Annual variations in marine environment may relate to foraging behaviour of parents at a given colony that affects the growth rate of chicks (Weimerskirchet al., 2001;Hedd et al., 2002;Quillfeldt et al., 2010) and therefore may influence the adult body size. The age was not known for the individuals measured in this study, and, therefore, any annual differences in fledgling size might be obscured: our body size index represents only the mean for each colony.

One striking finding in this study was that individuals at NA were significantly smaller than all other study colonies. NA is the only population breeding in tropical region among the study colonies. In tropical waters, surface food abundance is generally low, and resources are much less predictable due to less structured oceanographic features compared to temperate or polar region (Longhurst & Pauly, 1987;Weimerskirch, 2007). Hence, efficient gliders are believed to be favoured in tropical oceans due to their low flight costs when searching over large areas (Ashmole & Ashmole, 1967;Ballance & Pitman, 1999;Cairns et al. 2008). Theoretically, the surface area to volume ratio becomes larger with the decrease of body size (i.e. smaller bodied individuals are supposed to have larger wing relative to the volume). Hence, NA shearwaters could be specifically adapted to a tropical environment. Another possibility may be a large spatial gap (>950 km) between mainland populations (FO, SA, AW, KA, MI, UW and DA) and SakishimaIsland populations (located at the southernmost end of the Japanese Archipelago), including NA (Fig. 1).
Hence, there could be a possibility that NA shearwaters are genetically different from other mainland populations, potentially representing sub-species or even different species.

Recently, another species in the same genus (the Cory's shearwater) has been divided into two different species: the larger Cory's shearwater Calonectris borealis and the smaller Scopoli's shearwater C. diomedea (Gómez-Díaz et al. 2006, 2009), showing different foraging characteristics, one of which relates to wing loading (Navarro et al. 2009b).

In streaked shearwaters breeding on islands around Japan, the overall trend of the geographical variations in body size followed Bergmann's/James's rule. Our results therefore show that the rule may be applied to at least some seabirds, i.e. to species that forage in the marine realm.
